sections.figure_alt: A segment joining the two axis intercepts.
sections.body_md:
Conditional gradient, also called Frank-Wolfe, never projects onto the set. It asks a different subproblem: minimize the linear model built from the current gradient. On a polytope the minimum is attained at a vertex, so the subproblem is a linear minimization oracle. The next point is a convex combination of the current point and that vertex. Convexity of the set keeps the combination feasible.

On the probability simplex the vertices are the standard-basis vectors, and the linear value at a vertex is one gradient component. The oracle returns a vertex of a smallest component. If several components tie, any convex combination of those vertices is also a minimizer. On the \(\ell_1\) ball the vertices are the signed basis vectors. The oracle picks a coordinate of largest gradient magnitude and the sign opposite the gradient.

The fraction in the convex combination can be chosen by an exact line search along the segment, or by the open-loop schedule \(2/(k+2)\) with \(k\) counting from zero. The first fraction equals \(1\), a full step to the oracle's answer. Later fractions decrease toward zero and never exceed \(1\).

For a smooth convex objective on a compact convex set, that schedule yields a bound of order \(1/k\) on the function gap. With a curvature constant \(C_f\) the gap is at most \(2 C_f / (k + 2)\). The curvature constant is finite when the gradient is Lipschitz and the set is bounded. The inequality bounds \(f(x_k) - f^\star\), not the distance from \(x_k\) to a minimizer.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
The oracle and the update are
\[
s \in \arg\min_{u \in \mathcal{X}} \nabla f(x)^T u, \qquad x_+ = (1 - \gamma) x + \gamma s.
\]
The schedule \(\gamma_k = 2/(k+2)\) gives \(f(x_k) - f^\star \le 2 C_f / (k + 2)\). On the simplex, \(s\) is a basis vector at a smallest gradient component.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
On the simplex, start at \((1/5,\ 4/5)\) with gradient \((5,\ -1)\) and fraction \(2/5\). The smaller component is \(-1\), so the oracle returns \((0,\ 1)\). The new point is \(\tfrac35\) of the current point plus \(\tfrac25\) of the oracle point.

The kite weight is 0.4. The new second coordinate is \(\tfrac35 \cdot 4/5 + \tfrac25 = 22/25\). The new first coordinate is \(\tfrac35 \cdot 1/5 = 3/25\). Choosing the larger gradient component would have maximized the linear model.

The fraction \(2/5\) is not the value of \(2/(k+2)\) at \(k = 0\), which is \(1\). The decreasing schedule bounds the function gap.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Selecting the largest gradient component maximizes the linear model. The oracle minimizes it. A second slip is to describe the \(O(1/k)\) result as a bound on \(\lVert x_k - x^\star\rVert\). The inequality bounds the function gap. A third is to project the gradient step and call the result a conditional-gradient step. The subproblem here is linear, not a nearest-point problem. A fourth is to take a fraction larger than \(1\). The combination would leave the segment and can leave the set. A tie for the smallest component makes the whole minimizing face optimal, not a single vertex.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Minimizing the linear model of \(x^T A x\) on the unit sphere returns the normalization of \(-A x\), a step toward a bottom eigenvector. The power method normalizes \(A x\) instead. The sphere is not convex, so that step replaces the vector rather than taking a convex combination. The second-mode coefficient contracts by \(|\lambda_2 / \lambda_1|\), and the Rayleigh error uses the square of that factor.
